transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-03-21 15:00 PST
Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Chang Wu (Redwood Product), Jacob Lee (NexaHealth CTO), Marta Ruiz (NexaHealth ML Eng), Samir Patel (NexaHealth Security), Aisha Khan (NexaHealth PM)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focused on where to place safety filters/moderation in Redwood's inference pipeline, tradeoffs on latency/throughput, KV cache and batching interactions, quantization impacts, and implications for VPC/on-prem deployments. Action items and perf runs agreed.

Topics covered:
- Pre-generation vs post-generation moderation placement
- Impact on latency P95/P99 and throughput when moderation runs inline
- Effect on batching and KV cache hit rates
- Quantization effects on safety classifier accuracy and speed
- VPC/on-prem constraints (no external moderation calls, KMS, logging)
- Canary strategy, metrics to monitor (FP/FN, latency, cost)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: okay, thanks everyone for joining, we'll focus on the guardrails question, specifically moderation placement and how that affects perf, priya will run through the topology and then we'll go into numbers
[00:18] Priya: yeah hi all, so the two common places people put moderation are before generation, i.e. pre-check user input, or after generation to scrub outputs, there are hybrid approaches too like in-prompt constraints and token-level filters; each has a different perf profile
[00:35] Jacob: quick Q — our main concern is latency for live chat, p95 under 400ms is our goal, so we need to know if adding a moderation step will break that
[00:48] Priya: great, and that's definitely achievable but depends on whether moderation is synchronous and if it's an extra model call. If you run a separate moderation model synchronously before the generation call, you're adding an extra model latency slice — say 30 to 120ms depending on model size and whether it's hosted or local
[01:10] Marta: that 30-120ms, is that for small mod models? We plan to quantize our serving stack — does quantization make the moderations faster and preserve accuracy?
[01:25] Priya: ok so quantization can reduce latency a bit — 10 to 30% speedups on large GPUs with the right kernels — but for safety classifiers, we've seen it cause some calibration drift in a few cases, so recommended approach is: quantize the main generation model for cost, but keep safety models at higher precision (or at least validate on your prompt set)
[01:46] Samir: we can't call external APIs for moderation, everything has to stay inside our VPC, that's a hard req for us due to PHI; so how does on-prem or VPC change options?
[02:00] Priya: right, if you need in-VPC moderation then you either deploy a Redwood Private instance with the moderation model colocated, or run a lightweight classifier as a sidecar. That removes network egress but means we have to account for the extra GPU/CPU cost on your infra
[02:18] Chang: also worth noting, for dedicated pools we support colocated model variants so you can pin a moderation model and generation model to the same GPU pool which reduces inter-node transfer. But that affects capacity planning
[02:33] Alex: let's talk cache and batching: if you do pre-filtering on input text, you're blocking bad prompts before they hit the serving runtime, so you preserve KV cache integrity; if you only filter after generation you might waste tokens and compute for outputs that will be dropped
[02:52] Marta: but some of our policies require inspecting the generated text because a benign prompt can produce an unsafe completion due to model hallucination — so pre-filtering alone isn't sufficient
[03:08] Priya: exact, and that's why hybrid is often recommended: lightweight pre-filter to block egregious cases fast (low compute, high precision filter), then post-gen moderation with a stronger model for samples that pass pre-filter. Implementation detail: batch pre-filters very aggressively — they're usually cheap classifiers and can be batched to maintain throughput
[03:30] Jacob: how does batching interact with pre-filters? if we batch too much we hit higher latency but better TPS — would pre-filtering force smaller batches?
[03:42] Priya: pre-filters can be batched separate from generation. Typical pattern: gather N requests for pre-filter, run a small classifier, then only pass the allowed requests to the generation batch. So you can keep generation batch sizes high while keeping pre-filter latency low if you tune batch windows. The tradeoff is complexity and additional buffer memory for holding pending requests
[04:00] Alex: I want to call out KV cache behavior — KV cache improves autoregressive generation latency when you have repeated prefixes or multi-turn chat. If pre-filter rejects a prompt before it ever populates the cache, then cache hit rates may drop slightly for some flows, but overall it's cheaper because you never did the generation compute. Post-filtering means you populate cache and then potentially discard output; you may also need to invalidate or avoid caching content that was later flagged
[04:23] Marta: what about asynchronous moderation? Could we return the response to the user quickly and then retroactively remove or flag content if moderation fails?
[04:33] Priya: yes, async is a valid pattern for non-live-critical UIs. It reduces perceived latency but introduces complexity for UX and compliance — some customers can't accept that because of PHI or legal constraints. For chat systems where the worst case is a user seeing a bad line for a short time it's ok; for regulated health messaging, it's not acceptable
[04:52] Samir: for our use case we need synchronous blocking for certain categories and async for others — is Redwood able to support mixed policies?
[05:02] Priya: absolutely, route-by-policy is supported. You can tag requests and apply different pipelines: pre-filter-blocking for high-risk categories, post-filter-review for low-risk categories, and async audit for logging. Redwood's routing can fallback to a safer, smaller model variant if the main model is unavailable
[05:22] Alex: let's get into numbers we ran last week. We have two benchmark configs: 1) pre-filter + generation (both local) and 2) generation then post-filter. For a baseline gen-only p95 of 180ms on A2-class instance, adding a lightweight pre-filter added ~40ms p95, so total ~220ms. Post-filtering added ~60-80ms because it was a larger model run after generation, and wasted about 12% compute on average because some outputs got blocked
[05:52] Marta: that 12% wasted compute — is that consistent across traffic distributions?
[06:00] Priya: it varies. In seed tests with adversarial prompts we saw up to 30% waste; in normal product traffic it was closer to 8-12%. The important part is to measure on your prompt set, we can help run the canary
[06:15] Jacob: can batching hide the moderation latency?
[06:20] Priya: yes, if your pre-filter is batchable and you allow a small batching window, you amortize the cost. But remember p95 is sensitive to tail and to batching windows — you might need to tune batch sizing vs acceptability for latency. For very low-latency apps (<200ms p95) you need small batches and very lightweight pre-filters
[06:40] Alex: an operational idea — use a cheap heuristic first (regex, deny-list, simple classifier) that filters out obvious cases in under 10ms then fall back to model-based moderation for borderline cases. That preserves p95 for most traffic and keeps safety while reducing model calls
[06:57] Marta: regex/deny-list sounds good but we worry about false negatives — misses are bad for us
[07:05] Priya: yup that's why it's hybrid: regex catches explicit tokens, simple classifier catches patterns, and full model handles nuanced outputs. Also, you can run the full model asynchronously for audit or to retrain the simple classifier
[07:19] Chang: let's touch quantization again — for the full moderation model we recommend testing INT8 and FP16. INT8 gives best cost reductions but we've seen calibration issues in corner cases; for compliance-related categories keep FP16 or FP32 until validated. For the generation model, quantization is usually safe and provides good perf/cost tradeoffs
[07:42] Samir: how about accuracy numbers? do you have expected FP/FN rates for quantized moderation vs unquantized?
[07:50] Priya: ballpark — on our internal eval set, INT8 degraded recall by ~1-3 percentage points for some nuanced categories; precision remained similar. But that's highly model and category dependent. We'll share the benchmark sheet with per-category deltas
[08:05] Jacob: can Redwood run those moderation models in a separate dedicated capacity so it doesn't steal cycles from generation capacity?
[08:12] Alex: yes, for Dedicated or Private you can provision distinct GPU pools for moderation vs generation. We recommend separate pools for heavy post-gen moderation to avoid contention, and smaller dedicated pools for pre-filter classifiers or sidecars
[08:27] Marta: will that increase cost significantly? We're trying to optimize $/1M reqs
[08:33] Priya: cost increases do happen but it's about smart provisioning. If pre-filter is cheap you only need a small pool. For post-gen heavy checks, use autoscaling policies and prefer lower-cost instance types for the moderation model if latency budgets allow. Redwood Optimize can profile and recommend configurations to minimize unit cost while meeting SLOs
[08:52] Alex: regarding KV cache again — if you plan on long-running chat sessions with many turns, caching dramatically reduces token compute. For that use-case, pre-filtering early is preferred so you avoid polluting cache with flagged content. Also consider partial caching strategies where you mask flagged tokens from entering the cache
[09:12] Marta: masking sounds interesting — is that supported or would we need a custom hook?
[09:17] Priya: we have hooks. You can plug in a write-filter that modifies what gets cached. We can share the API doc.
[09:24] Jacob: what about auditing and logging for moderation decisions in VPC/offline mode? we need tamper-proof logs and ability to replay
[09:33] Priya: Redwood Private supports audit log exports to your S3 or logging endpoint, with signed timestamps. For tamper resistance, you can integrate with your KMS/HSM to sign entries. For hosted, we provide audit logs too but some customers with PHI prefer Private for full control
[09:46] Samir: any guidance on canarying moderation changes? we want to avoid rollout regressions
[09:52] Priya: yes, standard canary: run new moderation model in shadow mode first, compare flag rates and false positive/negative drift on a sampled set. Redwood Console has side-by-side evaluation and regression alerts tied to your eval prompts. Start with low traffic percentage (1-5%), monitor important metrics, then ramp
[10:12] Alex: quick note on fallback policies — if moderation model is slower or fails, you can fall back to a conservative policy (e.g., block or route to human review) depending on the risk profile. For chat, fallback to a smaller safe model is common to keep UX intact
[10:29] Marta: okay let's talk about a concrete pilot. We want synchronous blocking for high-risk categories, post-gen review for others, and all logs stored in our VPC. Can Redwood handle that for a pilot?
[10:40] Priya: yes. Proposed pilot: 2-week canary with 10% production traffic in your staging VPC. We'll deploy pre-filter sidecars and a dedicated post-gen moderation pool, run the redwood runtime with KV cache enabled, and measure p95/p99 and total cost. We'll instrument FP/FN and provide a comparison spreadsheet
[10:59] Jacob: perfect. Also we need samples — we'll share top 200 prompts and expected QPS which is currently ~150 rps peak
[11:08] Alex: that QPS number helps with batch sizing and pool sizing — with 150rps you can afford moderate batching but still need to tune for p95. We'll size test accordingly
[11:18] Priya: last technical bit — if you run moderation on GPU it costs more but reduces latency; CPU classifiers are cheaper but may increase latency for some models. For small classifier models, CPU is fine and can be scaled horizontally; for large nuanced classifiers GPU is better
[11:34] Marta: curious about dev experience — how much work to add custom rules and integrate with our RBAC?
[11:40] Chang: rule engine is pluggable. You can add deterministic rules (regex) and model-based rules. RBAC ties into your SSO via SAML and we map roles to who can modify policies. We also store policy versions so you can audit changes
[11:55] Samir: can we keep moderation telemetry separate from content logs for compliance?
[12:00] Priya: yes, you can choose logging destinations and retention per stream. Redwood Console exposes controls and we can restrict export locations for Private deployments
[12:12] Alex: wrap up with quick recap and next steps then open for any final questions
[12:17] Priya: recap — recommended hybrid approach: quick pre-filter (cheap) + post-gen model for nuanced cases; colocate moderation in VPC/Private if PHI is involved; separate GPU pools to avoid contention; test quantization carefully for moderation models; canary in shadow mode then ramp. We've got action items and a 2-week canary plan on the table
[12:35] Jacob: thanks this is actionable. No further technical Qs right now, we'll get the sample prompts and QPS to you
[12:45] Aisha: one small UX ask — if we go async for some categories, can Redwood provide a UX hook for retracting content or notifying users?
[12:52] Priya: yes, webhooks for audit and retraction are supported; you can also set TTLs for ephemeral content
[13:00] Alex: OK thanks all, we'll follow up with the sheet and schedule the in-VPC perf run.
